verdict: OK to lend in Ghaziabad engineering & capital goods — pursue order-backed OEM and export-linked component makers, avoid EPC and payment-stressed units.
title: Ghaziabad Engineering & Capital Goods: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**These units convert steel, castings and bought-out components into machinery, structures and job-work parts, and cash comes back only after the buyer accepts and pays.** Value sits in the order book and the customer relationship, not the shop floor; the fixed asset is modest but the working-capital cycle is long, and for EPC-style work the cash conversion cycle runs higher than for OEMs [11]. So when a proposal lands, check the order book and buyer profile first; if the order book is thin or single-buyer, ask for the last twelve months of dispatch and payment records.

## What has changed now
**The demand signal is genuinely strong: IIP for NIC 28 is +10.3% YoY and +10.4% Apr-to-date, and exports are +19.8% Apr-to-date in USD [D].** Uttar Pradesh GST is running +14.2% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1% [D], so Ghaziabad is pulling ahead of the national average. But local reporting says industrialists are protesting lack of facilities and restrictive policies [1], while a second local report frames policy reform as the fix [2]. **Read that as demand good, execution environment uneven.**

## Where the growth is
**Pursue component and structure makers feeding power transmission, railways, data centres and export buyers.** Skipper posted its highest-ever Q2 revenue with PAT up 56% and strong export growth [6]; DEE's order book crossed Rs 1,300 crore with revenue up 77% YoY to Rs 286.7 crore [5]; Pitti cites AI data-centre power needs and global sourcing consolidation as structural demand [4]. Ghaziabad entrepreneurs reportedly booked Rs 18 crore of domestic and overseas orders at a UP trade show [3] — small, but it shows export enquiry is reaching this cluster. **Avoid pure EPC and single-client job-work units**, where the cash conversion cycle is longest [11].

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the order book, not the balance sheet.** Take monthly stock and book-debt statements, monthly GST returns, and quarterly order-book position with buyer names. Ask for bank guarantees where bidding is involved [9]. Where margins are thin — Suzlon grew revenue 26% YoY to Rs 4,869 crore but EBITDA margin fell to 14.8% from 18.6% [7] — price for that and cap drawing power at a realistic margin. **Collect from customer** the local receivable days and capex plans; the sources do not give Ghaziabad-specific figures.

## Early warning signs
**Watch receivable days stretching beyond the stated credit terms, order book that does not convert to dispatch, and rising payables masking a longer cycle [11].** A buyer concentration above half of monthly billing, or GST turnover falling below bank-statement credits, means stop and re-assess. Local sources are thin on Ghaziabad-specific credit data, so lean on first principles and these peer signals.
watch: Monthly GST returns vs bank credits
GST turnover below bank credits for two months -> ask for buyer-wise ledger and hold enhancement
Order book flat while inventory rises -> reduce drawing power
Receivables beyond stated terms by 15 days -> seek fresh buyer confirmation
Single buyer above 50% of billing -> cap exposure and seek diversification plan
Fresh protest or restriction reported [1] -> pause new sanctions in affected estates
